Article Title: From E coli to amenity gaps: What CAG found beyond the railway makeover
Article Text:
Vande Bharat to E. coli: What CAG found behind Indian Railways’ big makeover (PTI file photo)

Amenities gap at railway stations (Source: CAG)

What the CAG found at railway stations

Water quality emerges as a key concern

The missing link in the makeover

Record spending, 98.4% operating ratio

Building big, maintaining better

A financial makeover still in progress

Freight down, passenger revenue misses target

The real makeover begins after inauguration

From showcase projects to everyday reliability

Record capex, heavy government support: The financial reality behind Railways’ makeover

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Indian Railways is in the middle of one of its biggest modernisation drives, spanning station redevelopment, new trains, electrification and record capital investment. A recent CAG audit, however, shows that alongside this expansion, gaps remain in some of the most basic passenger amenities at stations.For years now, the story of Indian Railways has been told through images of transformation.There are sleek Vande Bharat trains gliding out of revamped stations, glossy artist's impressions of redeveloped railway hubs, new concourses, lifts, escalators and futuristic terminals. The government has steadily raised capital expenditure on the national transporter, presenting the Railways as one of the central pillars of country's infrastructure push.The makeover is visible. But the latest audit findings of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India show that ensuring basic passenger amenities remain available and functional across the network continues to be an important part of that transformation.In a report tabled in Parliament on August 12, the CAG examined passenger amenities and sanitation at non-suburban railway stations and found significant gaps in the basics.Of 512 stations covered by the audit, 458 had deficiencies in one or more essential passenger amenities. Water samples collected from coolers at eight stations were found contaminated with E. coli, a marker that raises serious concerns about faecal contamination and water safety.The latest CAG reports, including those on passenger amenities, railway finances and compliance, raise a larger question about the makeover that we keep talking about: Is the transformation merely about building new assets, or is it also about making the everyday railway experience safer, cleaner, more reliable and financially sustainable?Indian Railways is not a conventional transport system. It is the daily infrastructure of a country on the move.Millions pass through its stations not as occasional tourists but as workers, students, migrants, families and small traders. For many, the railway journey begins long before boarding a train. It begins with finding the platform, locating a toilet, getting drinking water, sitting in a waiting area and navigating a crowded station.That is precisely where the latest audit becomes very important.The CAG's Report No. 31 of 2026, focused on passenger amenities and sanitation at non-suburban railway stations, was tabled on August 12.The findings suggest that while major infrastructure projects may dominate the narrative around railway modernisation, there continues to be significant variation in the availability of basic passenger amenities across the stations examined.The audit found deficiencies at nearly nine out of every 10 stations examined.The gaps ranged across basic amenities such as toilets, urinals and drinking-water facilities. In other words, the issue was not necessarily the absence of a grand redevelopment plan. It was ensuring that facilities passengers encounter every day are available and functional consistently.The audit underlines that station modernisation has two components: creating new infrastructure and ensuring that routine passenger amenities remain available and functional.Perhaps the most striking finding in the audit concerns drinking water.The CAG found E. coli contamination in samples collected from water coolers at eight locations. The presence of such bacteria raises concerns because contaminated drinking water can pose a serious public-health risk.The finding was particularly important because access to safe water is among the most basic services expected at a railway station.The finding has now prompted a special response from Indian Railways.The Railways has launched a special drive to clean and disinfect drinking-water tanks and filters. Zonal Railways have also been advised to undertake comprehensive inspections of drinking-water infrastructure and rectify deficiencies wherever they are found.Importantly, the exercise is not being limited to a one-time cleaning drive. The Railways has directed that station-wise deficiencies and the action taken to address them be monitored.That changes the nature of the response.The issue is no longer simply whether a station has a drinking-water facility. The bigger question is whether the entire system behind that facility, tanks, filters, pipelines, coolers and monitoring, is functioning properly and delivering safe water consistently.It is a crucial distinction.A water cooler installed at a station is an infrastructure achievement. Ensuring that the water remains safe every day is a maintenance and governance challenge.The new cleaning and inspection drive also underlines the broader problem identified by the CAG.Modernisation is not simply about creating infrastructure. It is about maintaining it.A water cooler installed at a station is only as useful as the quality of the water flowing through it. A new toilet is only as useful as its cleanliness and upkeep. An escalator that frequently stops working or a waiting hall that is not maintained does not become useful merely because the infrastructure exists.The challenge for Indian Railways is increasingly shifting from construction to maintenance.India's railway modernisation programme has been built around large numbers.New lines, doubling and electrification projects, station redevelopment, signalling upgrades and new rolling stock have become the visible markers of the transformation.The latest financial audit, Report No. 30 of 2026, was also tabled on August 12 and examines the finances of the ministry of Railways for the year ended March 2025. Its significance lies in placing the makeover against the larger question of financial capacity and the resources available to sustain such an ambitious transformation.The numbers show the scale of the continuing investment push. For 2026-27, railway capital expenditure is budgeted at Rs 2.93 lakh crore, with budgetary support from the Centre expected to finance around 95% of that spending.This represents a fundamental shift in how railway modernisation is being financed.The network is no longer relying only on internally generated resources to fund its massive expansion and upgrade plans. Government support has become the financial backbone of the capital programme.That has enabled Indian Railways to build faster. At the same time, the growing asset base makes maintenance, upgrade and efficient operation increasingly important.The answer lies partly in the operating ratio, a measure of how much of every rupee earned is consumed by working expenses. A lower operating ratio leaves more room for investment and financial flexibility.For 2026-27, the operating ratio is budgeted at 98.4%, after a revised estimate of 98.8% for 2025-26, as reported by Parliament and PRS Legislative Research.The margin remains narrow.The modernisation drive is also being supported by a substantial increase in central budgetary support. Government support is expected to finance around 95% of railway capital expenditure in 2026-27, while the operating ratio remains above 98%.The CAG's findings bring an old problem into a new context.The audit places renewed focus on maintenance, an increasingly important issue as the Railways adds and upgrades infrastructure across a very large network.The transformation of Indian Railways will not be judged only by whether a station redevelopment project is completed on schedule. It will also be judged years later by whether the facilities created continue to work as intended.The CAG examined precisely these everyday indicators — drinking water, toilets and urinals, seating, platform shelters, accessibility and sanitation — making the report as much about service quality as infrastructure availability.The findings highlight the importance of pairing asset creation with regular maintenance, inspection and service monitoring.The former is visible. It can be photographed, inaugurated and counted.The latter is harder. It requires regular inspection, accountability, maintenance contracts, quality checks and systems that continue to work long after the inaugural ceremony.The Railways' latest drinking-water drive points in that direction. The focus on comprehensive inspection, rectification and station-wise monitoring suggests an attempt to make maintenance more systematic rather than waiting for individual problems to surface.The real test will be whether that monitoring continues after the immediate response to the audit findings.The challenge of maintaining standards across a vast networkThe latest findings also underline the challenge of ensuring uniform service standards across a railway network of India's scale.At one level are the flagship projects: High-profile trains, major stations and corridors receiving substantial investment. These are the symbols that shape public perception of a changing railway system.At another level are hundreds of ordinary stations where the provision and upkeep of basic amenities remain equally important.The CAG's examination of 512 stations and its finding of deficiencies at 458 suggests that ensuring minimum standards consistently across the network remains a work in progress.That is where the true test of the makeover lies.Indian Railways is too large and too geographically diverse for transformation to be measured only through a handful of showcase projects. The success of the modernisation programme will depend on whether improvements can eventually become the standard across the network rather than remain concentrated at major stations.The passenger boarding from a smaller city experiences the Railways through the condition of the local station.That station is where the promise of transformation ultimately becomes visible.The railway modernisation programme is also taking place against a difficult financial backdrop.Passenger and freight revenues remain central to the financial health of the system. Yet recent budget analysis has pointed to revenue estimates falling short of targets, even as the Railways continues to undertake large capital investments.According to the 2026-27 analysis by PRS Legislative Research, freight revenue in 2025-26 was estimated to be 5.1% below the budget estimate, while passenger revenue was expected to fall short by 13.8%.This does not mean that the railway transformation has stalled. Far from it. The scale of capital expenditure remains historically high.It does mean, however, that central budgetary support remains a major pillar of the current modernisation programme.The question is whether the investments being made today will eventually create a more efficient railway system, one that can carry more freight, attract more passengers, reduce congestion and improve revenue generation.That is the economic logic behind modernisation.The CAG's latest findings add another dimension: modernisation must also ensure that spending translates into reliable passenger amenities and services.There is another lesson in the CAG audit.One of the most important parts of railway transformation is creating systems capable of looking after the infrastructure once it is built.A station redevelopment project has a beginning and an end. A maintenance programme does not.It requires continuous supervision.The Railways' decision to launch a special drive for cleaning and disinfecting drinking-water tanks and filters, inspect infrastructure and monitor station-wise deficiencies is therefore significant.The Railways will now have to ensure that the response goes beyond corrective action after contamination is detected. The larger goal is preventive systems, regular water testing, routine cleaning and disinfection, replacement of ageing infrastructure, clear responsibility for sanitation, and stronger monitoring of passenger amenities.The same principle applies across the network.Modernisation must become a process rather than an event.The CAG's findings have arrived at an important moment because Indian Railways is entering a phase where the story can no longer be told only through the scale of capital expenditure. The network has already seen major investments and ambitious announcements.The next question is whether these investments are producing a railway that works better every day.There is no doubt that Indian Railways is changing.The infrastructure pipeline is enormous. Capital spending remains high. Stations and trains look different from what they did a decade ago. Electrification, new corridors and capacity expansion are reshaping the network.The CAG audit does not erase those changes.Instead, it adds another dimension to the modernisation story: the importance of ensuring that basic passenger services improve alongside major infrastructure creation.A transformed railway will ultimately be judged both by its new assets and by the consistency with which its everyday facilities work.It must be judged by outcomes.The latest audit reports offer precisely that reminder.The CAG's passenger amenities report was tabled in Parliament on August 12, alongside the latest reports on railway finances and compliance. Together, they offer a snapshot of a system undergoing one of its most ambitious periods of investment while still grappling with persistent questions of service delivery, maintenance and financial sustainability.The new drinking-water drive shows that the Railways is responding to at least one of those concerns. But whether the effort translates into consistently safer and better-maintained facilities across stations will determine its real impact.The railway makeover, in other words, is real. But seems unfinished.The CAG report does not negate the scale of the transformation underway in Indian Railways. Capital investment remains at record levels, stations are being redeveloped and capacity is expanding. What the audit adds to that picture is a reminder that the next phase of modernisation will also depend on maintenance, consistency and ensuring that facilities already created remain functional, accessible and safe.The Railways' response to the water-quality findings, including inspections, filtration upgrades and station-wise monitoring, shows that corrective action has begun. The larger test will be whether these systems can help close the remaining amenity gaps across a network that serves millions of passengers every day.For millions of passengers, transformation will ultimately mean something simple: a clean station, a functioning toilet, safe drinking water and a journey in which the infrastructure created for them continues to work as intended.
Article Summary: Indian railways is in the middle of one of its biggest modernisation drives, spanning station redevelopment, new trains, electrification and record capital investment. A recent cag audit shows that alongside this expansion, gaps remain in some of the most basic passenger amenities at stations.

Article Title: A Kansas cowboy put 50 wind turbines on his 7,000-acre ranch and turned the wind into his most reliable cash crop, selling electricity to thousands of homes
Article Text:
A Kansas cowboy turns 50 wind turbines into a new cash crop

Fifty turbines are part of a 100-turbine wind farm

Wind became a reliable source of ranch income

Cattle still graze around the turbines

The project brought wider economic benefits to the region

The wind became another cash crop without replacing the cattle

A 7,000-acre cattle ranch in Kansas has found an unusual way to generate a steady income alongside traditional ranching. Pete Ferrell, a fourth-generation rancher, hosts 50 industrial wind turbines on his property as part of the 100-turbine Elk River Wind Project, a 150-megawatt facility that began operating in 2005. The turbines do not replace the cattle or transform the entire ranch into an energy facility. Instead, cattle continue to graze across much of the tallgrass prairie while the wind project provides Ferrell with lease income. The facility also generates enough electricity to serve tens of thousands of homes based on its original production estimates. What began as a source of concern for Ferrell eventually became an important financial cushion, particularly during droughts when traditional ranching income can become unpredictable.The Ferrell family's connection to wind power began long before today's giant turbines appeared across Kansas. In 1923, Ferrell's great-grandfather installed a Jacobs Windjammer wind turbine paired with a Delco glass battery at the ranch, providing electricity before the electrical grid reached the property. Nearly a century later, Pete Ferrell faced a very different proposal when developers approached him about installing commercial wind turbines.He initially rejected the idea because he feared the machines would damage the prairie and interfere with the ranching operation. A visit to California's Altamont Pass changed his perspective after he saw ranchers continuing to care for their land while turbines operated around them. The experience helped convince Ferrell that wind energy could coexist with cattle ranching, eventually leading him to lease part of his property for the Elk River Wind Project.The 50 turbines on Ferrell's property represent only half of the Elk River Wind Project. Kansas state records describe the facility as a 150-megawatt wind farm containing 100 GE 1.5-megawatt turbines in Butler County near Beaumont. The remaining turbines are located on neighbouring properties. The project began commercial operation in December 2005 and was originally expected to generate about 550,000 megawatt-hours of electricity each year. At the time, developers estimated that output would be equivalent to the electricity consumption of roughly 42,000 homes annually. The actual amount of electricity produced varies depending on wind conditions, so the figure should be understood as an annual estimate rather than a fixed number of homes receiving power directly from Ferrell's turbines. The electricity enters the regional power system, while Ferrell receives income from leasing his land to the project.The biggest attraction for Ferrell was not simply the electricity produced by the turbines but the additional income generated by leasing his land. Wind royalties have become an important part of the ranch's finances, providing a source of revenue that does not depend directly on cattle prices, grass production or rainfall. Ferrell has described wind as his "best insurance policy" because the payments continue even during difficult agricultural years. Drought can reduce forage across the Flint Hills and force ranchers to reduce livestock numbers or spend more money on feed, while the turbines can continue producing electricity as long as suitable winds are available. The arrangement effectively allows the same land to generate two forms of economic value. Cattle continue to provide the traditional agricultural income, while the wind project provides lease payments. The Environmental Defense Fund has highlighted Ferrell's experience as an example of how renewable-energy development can provide financial stability for rural landowners. Since the Elk River project began operating in 2005, wind royalties have accounted for roughly half of Ferrell's annual income, according to the Environmental Defense Fund, giving the ranch a more predictable source of revenue during difficult agricultural years. Wind leases can also provide landowners with long-term contractual income, with payments generally continuing for the life of a project rather than depending on the annual performance of a cattle operation. For ranchers facing volatile livestock markets and increasingly unpredictable weather, that predictable revenue can make renewable-energy leases an important form of financial diversification.The presence of 50 industrial turbines has not ended the ranch's traditional agricultural operation. Cattle continue to graze across much of the property, including areas surrounding the turbine infrastructure. Ferrell has said that roughly 50 acres of the ranch became unavailable for grazing because of turbine foundations, roads and related infrastructure. That represents only a small portion of a property covering about 7,000 acres. The arrangement allows Ferrell to maintain cattle production while earning additional revenue from the wind project. This is particularly significant in the Flint Hills, where ranching depends heavily on the health of native tallgrass prairie and seasonal weather conditions. Wind development therefore became an additional layer of income rather than a replacement for agriculture. Ferrell's experience shows why some rural landowners view turbines differently from people who see them only as large industrial structures. On a working ranch, the infrastructure can occupy a relatively small part of the property while providing payments over many years. The Environmental Defense Fund reports that individual turbines typically occupy less than an acre, allowing cattle and other ranch activities to continue around much of the wind infrastructure.Elk River is part of Kansas's much larger wind-energy industry, which has brought significant investment and lease payments to rural communities. Wind projects can generate revenue for landowners while also contributing to local tax bases, construction activity and employment. Kansas has become one of the leading wind-energy states in the US because of its strong wind resources and large areas of relatively open land. The economic benefits, however, come alongside genuine debates about where turbines should be built. Residents and landowners can raise concerns about views, wildlife, noise, roads, transmission infrastructure and changes to rural landscapes. Those issues are particularly important in the Flint Hills because the region contains some of the largest remaining areas of tallgrass prairie in North America. Ferrell's experience should therefore not be treated as evidence that every ranch is suitable for wind development. Instead, it shows how carefully planned projects can coexist with agricultural operations and give landowners another source of income.Nearly two decades after the Elk River Wind Project began operating, Ferrell's ranch remains a working cattle operation with 50 turbines standing across its prairie. The electricity generated by those turbines is sold into the regional power system, rather than directly by Ferrell to individual households, while his income comes from leasing his land to the wind project. That distinction does not make the financial transformation any less remarkable. The ranch has effectively found a way to make the same landscape produce two different sources of economic value. Cattle still depend on grass, rainfall and market conditions, while the wind turbines provide a separate stream of lease revenue. The arrangement also reflects a much longer family relationship with wind power that began with a small turbine and battery in 1923. Almost a century later, the Ferrell family is still drawing value from the Kansas wind, only now on a vastly larger scale.
Article Summary: Pete ferrell, a fourth-generation rancher, hosts 50 industrial wind turbines on his property as part of the 100-turbine elk river wind project. The turbines do not replace the cattle or transform the entire ranch into an energy facility. Instead, cattle continue to graze across much of the tallgrass prairie while the wind project provides ferrell with lease income.

Article Title: Weaker rupee may push foreign assets above FAST-DS Rs 1 crore limit: Taxpayers could lose the disclosure window which allows lower 60% tax outgo and face a steeper income tax bill
Article Text:
Since the tax payable through an updated return could be higher, an assessee may potentially save Rs 30-40 lakh.

What is the foreign asset disclosure scheme about?

Updated Income Tax Returns in Focus

Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS): FAQs

Below are some Frequently Asked Questions answered by the Income Tax Department about the new scheme:

What is the amount payable for a declaration under Section 133 – (Table: Sl. No. 2)?

What is the amount payable if the aggregate value of the assets located outside India is Rs 6.5 crore?

Income tax alert! If you have foreign assets then you need to be mindful of the negative impact on your tax outgo that the recent decline in rupee’s value versus the US dollar could have had.The Income Tax Department has announced a one-time voluntary disclosure window, which opened on August 16. It allows individuals to regularise their overseas shares, properties, ESOPs, dividends, interest and other such assets by paying 60% in tax and penalty, for amounts up to 1 crore.In fact, the rupee’s decline over the years, strict valuation requirements and the fact that many amounts exceed the prescribed lower limits are discouraging several taxpayers from disclosing previously unreported foreign income and assets.The rules specify March 31, 2026 as the exchange-rate date for converting the value of dollar-denominated assets into the Indian rupee, but do not clearly state which date should be used for converting foreign incomeWith the rupee having declined by 14-33% over three to seven years, many taxpayers could find that their holdings cross the 1 crore threshold if March 31 is used for the currency conversion. And that is the reason for them to worry about a higher tax outgo.There are, however, differing views on the issue.Ved Jain, former ICAI president, said that under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Rules, 2015, the valuation date for an undisclosed foreign asset is the date on which the asset comes to the assessing officer’s notice.He told ET that the scheme therefore takes March 31, 2026 as the valuation date for income as well, providing clarity on eligibility and the calculation of tax and penalty.Chartered accountant Ashish Karundia, however, takes a different view.“Undisclosed foreign income means income from a source outside India that was chargeable to tax in India but not offered to tax under the 1961 I-T law. The starting point is to determine how that income would have been computed and offered to tax under existing law. This requires reference to the I-T Rules, 1962, including Rule 115, which prescribes conversion of foreign-currency income. Thus, the applicable rate is the one that prevailed during the year income was earned,” he told the newspaper.Now, taxpayers with undisclosed income of over Rs 1 crore, such as Rs 2 crore, are looking at ways to use both an ‘updated return’ and the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS).Since the tax payable through an updated return could be higher, an assessee may potentially save Rs 30-40 lakh.The Rs 1 crore ceiling has created an incentive to divide undisclosed income between an updated return and FAST-DS, by declaring the amount above Rs 1 crore through the updated return and using FAST-DS for the remaining amount, said chartered accountant Harshal Bhuta.Although the approach may appear beneficial because of a tax difference of up to 40%, as well as immunity from penalty and prosecution, Bhuta warned that a FAST-DS declaration could be considered void if authorities find misrepresentation or suppression of facts. This could leave the taxpayer without recourse later, he said.The scheme is intended to give assessees an opportunity to rectify genuine errors. It permits the declaration of foreign assets worth up to Rs 5 crore that were acquired using tax-paid money by residents under the liberalised remittance scheme, as well as by returning NRIs who failed to disclose foreign accounts. However, the valuation provisions can lead to unexpected outcomes.For several categories of foreign assets, the value is generally determined as the higher of the acquisition cost or market value. “If an overseas asset bought for 5.25 crore is today worth only 3 crore, its value for the scheme may still remain 5.25 crore. The taxpayer could therefore fall outside the scheme,” said advocate Priyanshi Chokshi.If the required valuation has not been carried out, the indexed cost of acquisition is treated as the deemed fair market value. For instance, a property purchased for Rs 4 crore may currently be worth Rs 3.5 crore, but if its indexed cost is Rs 5.2 crore, that higher figure could push the taxpayer beyond the Rs 5 crore eligibility limit.“In borderline cases, valuation is not merely a compliance exercise. It could decide eligibility itself. Some clarification on falling-value assets and borderline cases would help,” said Chokshi.It is a one-time voluntary disclosure scheme contained in Chapter IV (sections 130 to 144) of the Finance Act, 2026. It enables eligible taxpayers to declare certain undisclosed foreign assets, undisclosed foreign income, or undeclared foreign assets, on payment of a specified tax or fee.The Scheme comes into force on 16th August, 2026.The last date has been fixed as 31st December, 2026. No declaration can be filed after this date.The valuation date is 31st March, 2026. The fair market value of assets proposed to be declared must be computed as on this date.The “income-tax authority” for the purposes of the Scheme is the Principal Director General of Income-tax (Systems) or the Director General of Income-tax (Systems), as the case may be. The entire process will be done online.The total amount payable would be the aggregate of - (i) tax of 30% of the value of the undisclosed asset located outside India or 30% of the undisclosed foreign income declared; and (ii) amount equal to the tax paid in (i)Where an undisclosed foreign bank account is valued at Rs 60 lakh and undisclosed foreign income is Rs 20 lakh, the aggregate payable is Rs 48 Lakh as given belowA flat fee of Rs 1 lakh, provided the aggregate value of the assets located outside India does not exceed Rs 5 crore.If the value of the assets is more than Rs 5 crore, the assessee will not be eligible to avail the scheme.
Article Summary: The income tax department has announced a one-time voluntary disclosure window, which opened on august 16. It allows individuals to regularise their overseas shares, properties, esops, dividends, interest and other such assets by paying 60% in tax and penalty.

Article Title: Budget: Budget proposes 30% TDS on net winnings in online games, removes threshold for TDS levy
Article Text: NEW DELHI: The government on Wednesday proposed to impose a 30 per cent tax on net winnings from online gaming and also do away with the existing threshold limit of Rs 10,000.The Budget 2023-24 proposed to introduce two new provisions for Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on online gaming -- levy of 30 per cent on payment of net winnings in a financial year and removal of the current Rs 10,000 threshold for the levy of TDS.In case the amount is not withdrawn from user account, tax shall be deducted at source at the end of the financial year.Speaking to reporters after the Budget, Revenue Secretary Sanjay Malhotra said the tax would be on net winnings on the aggregate value."When you take out the money from the winning accumulated pool, the withholding tax would be levied on that," Malhotra said.The other change in the TDS provision for online gaming was removing the Rs 10,000 threshold.Malhotra said the move came after it came to the notice of the tax department that some online gaming companies were keeping the winning amount lower than the threshold so that they are not covered under the TDS provision.Nangia Andersen LLP Partner Sudin Sabnis said online gaming has assumed gigantic proportions in India with revenue of Indian mobile gaming industry expected to reach $5 billion by 2025 and has been a subject matter of intense government scrutiny in the recent past from GST and Income Tax perspective."The Budget seeks to introduce a withholding tax on entire net winnings of any such user of online gaming platform. The gaming industry would need to revamp its strategy as these provisions along with ongoing discussions in GST Council could impact the user psyche similar to taxation of crypto currencies introduced in the last Budget," Sabnis said.Tax and consulting firm AKM Global, Tax Partner Amit Maheshwari said two new sections have been proposed with respect to online gaming Section 115BBJ to tax such proceeds at 30 per cent and Section 194BA providing TDS on net winnings in the user account at the end of the financial year."Additionally, certain definitions have been provided such as computer resource', 'internet', 'online game', 'online gaming intermediary', 'user', 'user account' in order to avoid ambiguity," Maheshwari said.
Article Summary: Budget 2023-24 proposed to introduce two new provisions for tax deducted at source (tds) on online gaming. Levy of 30 per cent on payment of net winnings in a financial year. Removal of the current rs 10,000 threshold for the levy of tds.

Article Title: Govt examining Supreme Court order on employees' pension scheme: Union minister Rameswar Teli
Article Text: NEW DELHI: The government on Thursday said it is examining a Supreme Court judgement which upheld Employees' Pension (Amendment) Scheme, 2014 and allowed employees to opt for enhanced pension coverage alongside their employers in four months' time."Yes, sir. The directions of the Supreme Court in the judgment are under examination," minister of state for labour & employment Rameswar Teli said in a written reply to Rajya Sabha.Teli was replying to a question on whether the government is aware about the Supreme Court verdict of November 4 on EPF pension scheme and by when it will implement the verdict and instruct the EPFO (Employees Provident Fund Organisation) to take actions for giving higher pension.In another written reply, Teli said the court judgement has legal, financial, actuarial and logistical implications.The scheme has provided for an extension of four months' time for eligible employees to opt for enhanced pension.The apex court order provides that employees who were existing EPS-95 members as on September 1, 2014 can contribute up to 8.33 per cent of their actual salaries, as against 8.33 per cent of the pensionable salary capped at Rs 15,000 a month, towards pension.It had also struck down the requirement in the 2014 amendments mandating employer contribution of 1.16 per cent of the salary exceeding Rs 15,000 per month.This will facilitate the subscribers to contribute higher to the scheme and get enhanced benefits accordingly.There are more than six crore subscribers of the retirement fund body. A large number of contributing members of the pension scheme would benefit from opting for contribution on wages higher than threshold of Rs 15,000 per month.The minster also said EPFO has a corpus of Rs 18,64,136 crore. This amount consists of Rs 11,37,096.72 crore in Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952; Rs 6,89,210.72 crore in Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 and Rs 37,828.56 crore in Employees' Deposit-Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976, as on March 31, 2022.
Article Summary: Rameswar teli says the directions of the supreme court in the judgment are under examination. He was replying to a question on whether the government is aware about the verdict of november 4. The apex court order provides that employees who were existing eps-95 members as on september 1, 2014 can contribute up to 8.33 per cent of actual salaries.
